prompt: Why does a dimension need a policy for change when a fact does not?
hint: What happens to a sale after it happens?

choices.text: A fact is fixed; a dimension keeps living
choices.why: Right. The sale stays true; the customer moves.

choices.text: Facts are smaller
choices.why: Size has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: Facts are loaded every night and dimensions once
choices.why: Both are loaded on a schedule; dimensions change between loads.

choices.text: Dimensions have no surrogate keys
choices.why: They do; that is what makes type 2 possible.

prompt: Match each SCD type to what it does on a change.

pairs.right: Adds a row for the new version
Moves the old value to a previous column

prompt: Which attribute is a natural type 0?

choices.text: The tier the customer has now
choices.why: It changes, and the shop analyses its changes.

choices.text: The city the customer lives in
choices.why: It changes; lesson 1 measured what that does.

choices.text: The day the customer joined
choices.why: Right. True once, and true forever.

choices.text: The customer's e-mail address, which people replace now and then
choices.why: It changed 825 times in the log.

prompt: How many of the 40,000 customers no longer live in the state they joined in?
A type 1 report of 2024 sales by state was run in October 2025 and again in December 2025, and the numbers differ. Why?

choices.text: Some 2024 sales arrived late
choices.why: The fact table did not change between the two runs.

choices.text: People who moved took their history to the new state
choices.why: Right. The overwrite rewrites the past to look like the present.

choices.text: Rounding in the second run
choices.why: R$ 9,392.24 is not rounding.

choices.text: December's extract had new customers
choices.why: New customers joined after 2024; they bought nothing then.

prompt: For which change is type 1 the right choice?
hint: Was the old value ever true?

choices.text: A customer moves from Curitiba to Recife
choices.why: Both cities were true in turn; sales by region need both.

choices.text: A reader is promoted to regular
choices.why: The programme is analysed by tier over time: type 2.

choices.text: A shop is moved to a different sales region
choices.why: The old region was true; type 2 or 3.

choices.text: A name mistyped at the till is corrected
choices.why: Right. The old value was never true, so there is no history worth keeping.

prompt: Under type 1, 2024 sales in Minas Gerais were R$ 4,688,508.55 in October and R$ 4,679,116.31 in December. By how many reais did the past move?
Customer 1 has three rows in `dim_customer`. What distinguishes them?
hint: Look at the dates and the tier.

choices.text: Three customers share the id by mistake
choices.why: It is one customer, in three periods.

choices.text: They are duplicates that the nightly load forgot to remove
choices.why: They differ in tier and period on purpose.

choices.text: Versions of one customer, each with its period
choices.why: Right. Reader, regular, patron, one after the other.

choices.text: One row per shop the customer used
choices.why: Shops are another dimension.

prompt: Why does the last version end on 9999-12-31 rather than on an empty value?
hint: Write the lookup for time t.

choices.text: One condition then serves the current row too
choices.why: Right. One condition, no special case.

choices.text: DuckDB rejects an empty timestamp in a column it has to compare
choices.why: It accepts them; the problem is the query.

choices.text: The customer will leave in 9999
choices.why: It is a far-away date standing for "not ended", not a prediction.

choices.text: To mark the customer as deleted
choices.why: The opposite: it marks the version that is still true.

prompt: Type 2 took the customer dimension from 40,000 rows to 49,309. By what percentage did it grow? Give one decimal.
Readers bought R$ 35.7 million in 2025 as readers, and today's readers bought R$ 34.4 million. Which number answers "how much does the lowest tier buy?"

choices.text: R$ 34.4 million, by today's tier
choices.why: That counts promoted customers' reader-era purchases elsewhere.

choices.text: Their average, about R$ 35.1 million
choices.why: An average of two different questions answers neither.

choices.text: Neither, without a type 3 column
choices.why: Type 2 answers it directly.

choices.text: R$ 35.7 million, by tier at the time of the sale
choices.why: Right. Each sale is grouped by the version it points at.

prompt: Where in Ana's warehouse is the "which version was true when this sale happened?" lookup done?

choices.text: In every report, with a date range join
choices.why: Reports join on the key; the range was used once.

choices.text: Once, when the load gives the fact its key
choices.why: Right. The time travel is paid once, and every query gets "as it was" free.

choices.text: In the report tool, which filters `is_current`
choices.why: That would give "as it is now", the other question.

choices.text: In PostgreSQL, before the extract
choices.why: The operational database keeps only the current state.

prompt: Put the steps of `13_dim_customer.sql` in order.
hint: First values, then the changes, then fill forward, then keys.
items: Find what each field held when the customer joined
List each moment a tracked field changed
Carry each field's last value forward and end each version at the next one
Assign surrogate keys and add the unknown member
trap: Assigning keys before the versions exist is the slip: there would be nothing yet to give a key to.

prompt: A move changes the city and the state. Why are they one moment, not two versions?
hint: Think of a version with the new city and the old state.

choices.text: Split, they would describe a place that never existed
choices.why: Right. "Curitiba, SP" would be a version that never existed.

choices.text: DuckDB merges rows with the same customer automatically
choices.why: Nothing is merged automatically; the query groups by moment.

choices.text: Cities are type 1
choices.why: The city is type 2 here.

choices.text: States are not tracked
choices.why: They are tracked, with the city.

prompt: What does step 2 of `load_month.sql` do to a customer whose tier changed?

choices.text: Deletes the old row
choices.why: Facts point at it; nothing is deleted.

choices.text: Overwrites the tier on the current row
choices.why: That would be type 1.

choices.text: Ends the current version on the extract's date
choices.why: Right. Step 3 then opens a new current version.

choices.text: Nothing; changes wait for the next month
choices.why: They are applied in the month they appear.

prompt: Why does step 2 compare with `IS DISTINCT FROM` rather than `<>`?

choices.text: It is faster
choices.why: Speed is not the reason.

choices.text: Two empty values count as equal, so no false change
choices.why: Right. With `<>`, a NULL compared to anything is unknown, and the row is skipped.

choices.text: `<>` does not work on text in DuckDB
choices.why: It does.

choices.text: It also compares the customer's name
choices.why: The name is not in the comparison; it is type 1.

prompt: November's load opened 1,214 versions and closed 263. How many of the opened versions were customers who joined during October?
A load that can run twice and leave the same result as running once is called ___.
What can type 3 not do that type 2 can?

choices.text: Show the previous value
choices.why: That is exactly what type 3 shows.

choices.text: Keep one row per customer, as type 1 does
choices.why: Type 3 does keep one row per customer.

choices.text: Run in DuckDB
choices.why: It ran in the lesson.

choices.text: Remember a second move
choices.why: Right. A second move loses the first city, and no sale knows which column applied.

prompt: The shop redraws its sales regions and wants every report to show old and new side by side for a while. Which type fits best?

choices.text: Type 0
choices.why: It would keep only the original region.

choices.text: Type 1
choices.why: It would leave only the new arrangement.

choices.text: Type 3: a region and a previous_region column
choices.why: Right. Its classic use is one reorganisation.

choices.text: A factless fact table
choices.why: Regions describe shops; they are not events.

prompt: What does a type 6 dimension add to type 2?

choices.text: Today's value on every row
choices.why: Right. Tier at the time and tier today, in one row.

choices.text: A sixth fact table, for changes
choices.why: The number is not a count of tables.

choices.text: Six rows per customer
choices.why: The number of rows follows the changes.

choices.text: A mini-dimension for fast-changing attributes
choices.why: That is type 4.

prompt: How many reais did customers who were readers at the time of purchase, and are patrons today, spend in 2025?
hint: The last row of the type 6 query.

prompt: A bank updates a credit score band for 5 million customers every month. Why not make the band a type 2 attribute of the customer dimension?

choices.text: Credit scores are personal data
choices.why: They are, and the same is true of the customer dimension already.

choices.text: Bands cannot be compared over time
choices.why: They can; that is why the history is wanted.

choices.text: Type 2 only works on text attributes, and a band is a number range
choices.why: Type 2 works on any attribute.

choices.text: Too many rows; a mini-dimension stays small
choices.why: Right. Type 4: the fast attributes move to their own key on the fact.

prompt: Match each attribute of Ana's customer dimension to its treatment.
A utility company stores each customer's city only to know where to send the bill. Which type suits the city there?
hint: Does anybody analyse facts by it over time?

choices.text: Type 2, as in the bookshop
choices.why: The same attribute can get a different answer in a different business.

choices.text: Type 1: only the current address matters
choices.why: Right. The type follows the questions asked of it.

choices.text: Type 0
choices.why: The bill would go to an old address.

choices.text: Type 3
choices.why: Nobody needs the previous city beside the current one.

prompt: Which of these must hold for every customer in a correct type 2 dimension? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Exactly one current row
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: No two versions overlapping in time
choices.why: Yes. An overlap counts a sale twice.

choices.text: No gap between one version's end and the next one's start
choices.why: Yes. A gap drops a sale out of the join.

choices.text: At least two versions
choices.why: 32,542 customers rightly have one.

prompt: Customer 1225 moved on 28 November and changed tier on 30 November. What does the extract-based load record?
hint: It only sees midnight on the first of each month.

choices.text: One version, from 1 December
choices.why: Right. The coarser the snapshot, the more history is lost.

choices.text: Two versions, on 28 and 30 November
choices.why: That is what the change log gives, not the snapshot.

choices.text: Nothing, because two changes cancel out
choices.why: They do not cancel; they arrive together.

choices.text: An error, because two changes conflict
choices.why: The load accepts them without complaint.

prompt: A sale from 20 October is loaded on 3 November, after the customer was promoted on 1 November. Which version should its `customer_key` point at, and what does the lesson's load do?
hint: The load joins on the time of the order.

choices.text: The current version; the load uses `is_current`
choices.why: A load using `is_current` would do that, and be wrong.

choices.text: The unknown member, until the next month
choices.why: The customer is known; the version is too.

choices.text: The October one, found from the order's time
choices.why: Right. A late fact still gets the version true when it happened.

choices.text: Both versions, split in half
choices.why: A sale has one customer version, not a share of two.
